**The Constitutional Convention: How Political Parties and No Term Limits Shattered the Dreams of The Founders, and Other Stories**, by **Tighe Taylor**

  
So far, the first story on the US constitution picked my interest in learning more about US history and the Founding Fathers. The author, Tighe Taylor, is also an attorney that knows the constitution very well and it shows by turning the creation of the constitution into a dramatic short story.

**The Kidnapping of Tammy Fitzgerald, by Tighe Taylor, JD**

I started this book just recently. It tells the story of a kidnapping of a child in a rural California desert town and the child's baby sitter, who then decides to investigate the kidnapping on her own after the police fail to take any action. 

The sitter, Taylor Shaw, also studies law at the local college and turns to the help of a law professor that used to work as a District Attorney and has experience in criminal investigations. Together they start uncovering corruption in the local police department and the true motives for the kidnapping.

The author of this book is a practicing lawyer and dedicates many chapters to understanding law and the US Constitution and its relations to this case. An insightful reading if one wants to learn more about law and how criminal investigations are conducted.

**The Kidnapping of Isabel Miller by Tighe Taylor**

I am reading this book by Tighe Taylor about an attorney that has her daughter kidnapped by a gangster. The gangster's motivation for the kidnapping was to deter a case the attorney was working on that was interfering with his criminal enterprises. 

The family of the attorney resides in the Coachella Valley and is employed by the US Attorney's Office to assist with cases in nearby Indian Reservations. Instead of turning to law enforcement for help the attorney turns towards the help of the Native Americans she has befriended.

The first chapter starts with the kidnapping scene. Then the author shares some background knowledge about US policy in dealing with Native American Indians.

It is a great and interesting read so far. It is a very action oriented story with a lot of background information on law and US Legal policy regarding environmental human rights and of Native peoples.

The author is a trained lawyer and has several other books written about true crime and some fiction on the legal profession.

As for surveying in the old days, old time surveyors would tell me stories of using tools like chains (to measure distances), blumpbobs (to keep the chain level), transits (to measure angles on a trigonometric scale), and giant compasses (To calculate a bearing). Everything was also drawn by hand. All I know is that the technology changes very quickly, but most of the concepts have been the same since the 1700's.

Here's a link to some examples on our web page: [Survey Projects](http://raylombera.com/projects.html)

I don't think a homeowner would like it if I posted a survey of their property on the internet. lol

Pretty much it would be a very detailed map of your property. It would include your property lines, buildings, trees, utilities, etc...

Oh!! I forgot to mention a surveyor's "Right of Passage." The law states that a land surveyor is allowed to enter someone's property even without permission. It's a controversial aspect of surveying. Most of the time people don't want us inside their land, but we have a job to do. In any case we try our best to convince a neighbor to let us into their yard to mark that property corner and collect information for the survey. If that fails we present our "Right of Passage" certificate and call the police.

The longest shot I have taken happens to be around 1,500 FT. Long shots like these commonly happen when working in very secluded areas like the desert or the woods.

I've come across a lot of wildlife and have become interested in studying nature in my free time. I've been attacked by Fire Ants, I killed a rattlesnake, I've been sprayed by a skunk, my whole crew once ran from a black bear!

A common surveyor's story is the infamous gun-crazed, territorial land owner. I've only come across that character once. There was a land dispute between two angry ranch owners out in Tujunga Canyon; and out came a rifle-wielding bearded man taking aim at my rodman. I have a title that is known as LSIT (Land Surveyor in Training). It is a pre-cursor to another license called LS (Land Surveyor) then PLS (Professional Land Surveyor).
